Myth: Negative working capital is always a warning sign.
Fact: Negative working capital can mean customers and suppliers fund operations.
Why: Collecting from customers before paying suppliers can push working capital below zero by design, so check cash flow and payable trends before judging it.
Show when: Operating working capital (receivables + inventory − payables − other operating current liabilities) < 0

Myth: Working capital is just current assets minus current liabilities.
Fact: Analysts strip out cash and debt to isolate operating working capital.
Why: Cash and borrowings reflect financing choices, so removing them shows how much money everyday operations actually tie up.
Show when: Cash and short-term investments > 25% of current assets

Myth: A current ratio above 1 means liquidity is safe.
Fact: Current ratio can hide restricted cash and receivables that won’t be collected.
Why: Restricted cash, slow inventory and doubtful receivables all count as current assets but cannot reliably pay near-term bills.
Show when: Current ratio > 1 and quick ratio < 0.7

Myth: Rising inventory always means demand is strong.
Fact: Inventory growing faster than cost of sales can signal slowing sales.
Why: Stock piling up faster than it sells ties up cash and raises the chance of discounts or write-downs later.
Show when: Inventory growth > cost of sales growth for 2 consecutive years

Myth: Higher receivables simply reflect higher sales.
Fact: Receivables growing faster than revenue means customers are paying slower.
Why: Revenue is recorded when delivered, not when paid, so lengthening collection time turns reported sales into cash more slowly and adds default risk.
Show when: Receivables growth > revenue growth for 2 consecutive years

Myth: Paying suppliers later is a permanent source of funding.
Fact: Stretching payables gives a one-time cash lift that can reverse.
Why: Payable days can only lengthen so far, and if suppliers push back or terms normalise, the cash flows back out.
Show when: Days payable outstanding rising for 3 consecutive years

Myth: Growing sales always bring in more cash.
Fact: Growth usually absorbs cash into receivables and inventory first.
Why: A larger business must fund more customer credit and stock before sales convert to cash, so operating cash flow can lag profit.
Show when: Revenue growth > 15% and increase in operating working capital > 0

Myth: Profit means cash in the bank.
Fact: Profit and cash flow differ because of timing and non-cash items.
Why: Accounts record income and costs when earned or incurred, not when cash moves, so the two can diverge even in a healthy business.
Show when: Any company

Myth: A profitable company cannot go bankrupt.
Fact: Profitable firms can fail when cash runs out before bills are paid.
Why: Late-paying customers, cash-demanding suppliers or heavy debt payments can drain liquidity even while accounting profit is positive.
Show when: Net income > 0 and operating cash flow < 0

Myth: EBITDA is a stand-in for operating cash flow.
Fact: EBITDA ignores capex, working capital, tax and interest.
Why: Those items all use real cash, so a firm can report strong EBITDA yet convert little of it into free cash.
Show when: Operating cash flow < 50% of EBITDA

Myth: Depreciation drains cash every year.
Fact: Depreciation lowers profit but spends no cash that year.
Why: The cash left when the asset was bought; depreciation only spreads that cost over time, which is why it is added back on the cash flow statement.
Show when: Depreciation and amortisation > 8% of revenue

Myth: Negative free cash flow means a weak business.
Fact: Heavy investment can push free cash flow negative while operations generate cash.
Why: Free cash flow is measured after capex, so a firm building capacity can show negative figures even though its core operations are cash-positive.
Show when: Operating cash flow > 0, free cash flow < 0 and capex > depreciation

Myth: Capex hits profit the moment it’s spent.
Fact: Capex hits cash now and profit gradually through depreciation.
Why: Long-lived assets are capitalised and written off over their useful life, so cash leaves upfront while only a slice reaches the income statement yearly.
Show when: Capex > depreciation for 3 consecutive years

Myth: Free cash flow can’t exceed net income.
Fact: Asset-light firms can convert more than 100% of profit into cash.
Why: When capex is below depreciation and working capital releases cash, cash generated can exceed reported earnings.
Show when: Free cash flow > net income for 3 consecutive years and capex < depreciation

Myth: All debt is bad.
Fact: Moderate debt can lower a company’s overall cost of capital.
Why: Debt is usually cheaper than equity and interest is often tax-deductible, but too much raises distress risk and borrowing costs.
Show when: Total debt > 0 and EBIT ÷ interest expense > 5

Myth: Net debt shows everything a company owes.
Fact: Net debt hides gross borrowings behind cash balances.
Why: Cash can be spent, restricted or trapped in subsidiaries, while the borrowings still fall due on schedule.
Show when: Total debt > 0 and cash > 50% of total debt

Myth: Low debt-to-equity means debt is no risk.
Fact: Interest coverage shows whether earnings can carry the debt.
Why: Lenders are paid from earnings and cash flow, not book equity, so weak coverage matters even when leverage ratios look modest.
Show when: Debt ÷ equity < 0.5 and EBIT ÷ interest expense < 3

Myth: Debt is repaid out of profit.
Fact: Debt is repaid from cash, not accounting profit.
Why: Lenders need cash, so free cash flow against scheduled repayments, not net income, shows whether the debt is affordable.
Show when: Free cash flow < current portion of long-term debt

Myth: Leases aren’t really debt.
Fact: Leases are fixed commitments that behave like borrowings.
Why: Payments are due regardless of performance, and modern standards put most leases on the balance sheet as liabilities.
Show when: Lease liabilities > 20% of total debt including leases

Myth: Interest cover just above 1 is fine.
Fact: Coverage near 1 leaves almost no cushion for an earnings dip.
Why: If operating profit falls slightly, interest goes uncovered, forcing asset sales, new borrowing or fresh equity.
Show when: EBIT ÷ interest expense between 1 and 2

Myth: Interest added to the loan instead of paid costs nothing.
Fact: Interest added to the loan saves cash now but grows the debt.
Why: Unpaid interest is added to principal, so the balance and future interest rise even though no cash left this year.
Show when: Interest expense > cash interest paid by more than 25% for 2 consecutive years and total debt rising

Myth: Higher revenue means higher profit.
Fact: Revenue can rise while margins shrink.
Why: If costs grow faster than sales, each extra unit of revenue earns less, and profit can even fall despite growth.
Show when: Revenue growth > 0 and operating margin down year on year

Myth: Net profit margin tells the whole profitability story.
Fact: Net margin mixes operations with financing, tax and one-offs.
Why: Operating margin isolates the core business, so a big gap between the two shows non-operating items shaping the bottom line.
Show when: Pre-tax margin differs from operating margin by > 5 percentage points

Myth: Thin margins mean a poor business.
Fact: Thin margins plus fast asset turnover can earn strong returns.
Why: Return on assets is margin times asset turnover, so high sales per unit of assets can offset low profit per sale.
Show when: Net margin < 5% and revenue ÷ average total assets > 2

Myth: High ROE always means excellent operations.
Fact: Leverage can lift ROE without better operations.
Why: Funding assets with debt shrinks the equity base, so return on equity rises even when return on assets is unchanged.
Show when: ROE > 20% and total assets ÷ equity > 3

Myth: One year’s earnings show normal profitability.
Fact: One-off gains and charges distort earnings trends.
Why: Asset sales, restructuring costs, impairments and settlements don’t recur, so they can hide the profit the business normally earns.
Show when: Non-operating or one-off items > 10% of pre-tax income

Myth: A high gross margin guarantees a profitable business.
Fact: Overheads below gross profit can erase a high gross margin.
Why: Selling, admin and R&D costs are charged after gross profit, so a firm can keep most of each sale at first and still earn little.
Show when: Gross margin > 50% and operating margin < 10%

Myth: Equity value and enterprise value mean the same.
Fact: Enterprise value adds net debt and other claims to equity value.
Why: Enterprise value covers the operating business for all capital providers, while equity value is only the owners’ residual share.
Show when: Net debt > 20% of total assets

Myth: Enterprise value can never be below equity value.
Fact: A net cash balance puts enterprise value below equity value.
Why: Cash is a non-operating asset, so when cash exceeds debt, the operating business is worth less than the equity as a whole.
Show when: Cash and investments > total debt

Myth: A DCF gives one exact value.
Fact: Small changes in discount rate or growth move DCF value sharply.
Why: Terminal value often makes up most of a DCF, so slightly different long-term assumptions change the result a lot.
Show when: Any company

Myth: Book value is what a company is worth.
Fact: Book value reflects historical cost, not current market worth.
Why: Assets are carried at past purchase cost less depreciation, while market value reflects expected future cash flows.
Show when: PP&E > 50% of total assets

Myth: EV/EBITDA compares capital-heavy and light firms fairly.
Fact: EBITDA ignores capex, so heavy investors need extra scrutiny.
Why: Two firms with equal EBITDA can need very different reinvestment, so the multiple hides how much cash is truly left.
Show when: Capex > 15% of revenue

Myth: P/E works for every company.
Fact: P/E breaks down when earnings are negative or tiny.
Why: Price divided by near-zero or negative earnings gives meaningless numbers, so revenue or cash-flow multiples are used instead.
Show when: Net income ≤ 0 or net income < 2% of revenue

Myth: Debt levels don’t affect P/E comparisons.
Fact: P/E shifts with leverage; EV-based multiples are much less affected.
Why: Interest cost cuts earnings per share, while enterprise value and EBITDA both sit before financing, so two similar firms with different debt compare more fairly on EV multiples.
Show when: Total debt ÷ equity > 1

Myth: A DCF works equally well for every company.
Fact: DCF is least reliable when cash flows stay negative for years.
Why: Most of the value then sits in distant years, where forecasts are least dependable.
Show when: Free cash flow < 0 for 3 consecutive years

Myth: Fast growth always creates value.
Fact: Growth adds value only when returns beat the cost of capital.
Why: Expanding with returns below what the capital costs makes a firm bigger, not more valuable.
Show when: Revenue growth > 15% and ROIC falling for 2 consecutive years

Myth: Growing companies fund themselves from profits.
Fact: Fast growth often needs outside capital.
Why: Capex and working capital for expansion can exceed operating cash flow, forcing borrowing or new shares.
Show when: Revenue growth > 20% and free cash flow < 0

Myth: Acquired growth equals organic growth.
Fact: Acquired growth is bought; organic growth is built.
Why: Acquisitions add revenue immediately but cost cash or shares and create goodwill, so underlying growth should be judged separately.
Show when: Cash paid for acquisitions > 0 and goodwill up > 20% year on year

Myth: Growth rates stay constant as companies get bigger.
Fact: Growth tends to fade as companies scale.
Why: The same percentage needs ever larger absolute gains and markets saturate, so growth usually tapers over time.
Show when: Revenue growth declining 3 years in a row

Myth: Falling revenue always means a declining business.
Fact: Revenue can shrink while margins and profit improve.
Why: Dropping unprofitable products, customers or markets lowers sales but can raise profit.
Show when: Revenue down and operating margin up year on year

Myth: A high dividend payout means a strong company.
Fact: Very high payouts can mean few growth options or little buffer.
Why: Cash paid out isn’t reinvested, and a payout near earnings leaves little cushion if profits fall.
Show when: Dividends paid > 80% of net income

Myth: Dividends are paid from profit.
Fact: Dividends are paid from cash.
Why: Profit is an accounting figure, so a firm with earnings but little free cash flow must borrow or use reserves to pay.
Show when: Dividends paid > free cash flow

Myth: Cutting a dividend always signals distress.
Fact: Cuts can free cash for investment or debt repayment.
Why: Boards may redirect cash to other uses, so the cash flow statement shows whether a cut reflects stress or choice.
Show when: Dividends down year on year and capex or debt repayment up

Myth: Firms paying no dividends return nothing to owners.
Fact: Retained earnings and buybacks are other ways to deliver value.
Why: Cash kept in the business can fund growth, and buybacks return cash by shrinking the share count instead.
Show when: Dividends paid = 0 and net income > 0

Myth: Buybacks and dividends are the same thing.
Fact: Both return cash, but flexibility and per-share effects differ.
Why: Dividends go to every holder and are hard to cut, while buybacks are discretionary and raise remaining holders’ ownership share.
Show when: Dividends paid > 0 and share repurchases > 0

Myth: Buybacks always raise a company’s value.
Fact: Buybacks lift EPS by shrinking shares, not by creating value.
Why: Cash leaving the company lowers equity value too, so per-share gains depend on the price paid, and buybacks may only offset staff share issuance.
Show when: Share repurchases > 0 and share count change within ±1%

Myth: Accounting rules are identical worldwide.
Fact: Standards differ across countries on leases, inventory and development costs.
Why: Different reporting frameworks allow different treatments, so comparing firms across borders usually needs adjustments.
Show when: Any company

Myth: Goodwill is a cash-like asset.
Fact: Goodwill is the premium paid over acquired net assets.
Why: It can’t be sold separately and is written down if the acquisition underperforms, so large balances carry impairment risk.
Show when: Goodwill > 20% of total assets

Myth: Stock-based pay isn’t a real cost.
Fact: Equity pay costs owners through dilution.
Why: Issuing shares to staff shrinks existing owners’ share of the company, even though no cash leaves.
Show when: Stock-based compensation > 5% of revenue

Myth: Cash received equals revenue earned.
Fact: Cash received before delivery is a liability, not revenue.
Why: Customer prepayments sit as deferred revenue until the product or service is provided, so cash and revenue can differ.
Show when: Deferred revenue up > 15% year on year

Myth: Impairment charges mean cash was lost this year.
Fact: Impairments are non-cash write-downs of earlier spending.
Why: The cash left when the asset was acquired; the charge admits it is now worth less, cutting profit without a current-year outflow.
Show when: Impairment charge > 0

Myth: Inventory costing method doesn’t affect profit.
Fact: Costing methods shift reported profit when prices change.
Why: Methods assign different costs to goods sold, so gross profit and inventory value change even though physical stock is identical.
Show when: Inventory > 20% of total assets

Myth: Valuable brands and know-how show up on the balance sheet.
Fact: Self-built brands and know-how usually don’t appear as assets.
Why: Accounting records only verifiable costs, so valuable internally created intangibles are often missing and book value understates them.
Show when: R&D expense > 8% of revenue

Myth: Tax expense on the income statement equals tax paid.
Fact: Reported tax expense often differs from cash tax paid.
Why: Timing differences such as depreciation methods and loss carry-forwards create deferred taxes, so the two figures rarely match.
Show when: |Cash taxes paid − income tax expense| > 20% of income tax expense

Myth: Bank deposits should be analysed like ordinary corporate debt.
Fact: For banks, deposits are the raw material, not a financing choice.
Why: Banks take deposits and lend them on, so funding and operations are intertwined, which is why net debt and EV measures don’t suit them.
Show when: Deposits > 50% of total liabilities

Myth: EBITDA is a useful measure for banks.
Fact: For banks, interest is an operating cost, so EBITDA misleads.
Why: Interest expense is the cost of funds a bank lends out, so adding it back removes a core expense.
Show when: Interest expense > 30% of interest plus non-interest income

Myth: Faster loan growth always means a stronger bank.
Fact: Rapid lending growth can bring higher future credit losses.
Why: Recently written loans are less tested, and provisions often rise later if borrowers struggle.
Show when: Gross loans up > 15% year on year

Myth: A profitable bank can’t fail.
Fact: Banks can fail from funding stress even while profitable.
Why: Funding is mostly short-term deposits and borrowing, so lost confidence can drain cash before earnings matter.
Show when: Loans > 100% of deposits

Myth: Loan loss provisions are a minor routine item.
Fact: Provisions for expected loan losses can swing a bank’s profit sharply.
Why: They are deducted from operating profit before tax, so rising expected losses cut profit even if interest income grows.
Show when: Provision for credit losses > 20% of net interest income

Myth: Rising interest rates always help banks.
Fact: Banks earn the gap between lending and funding rates.
Why: If funding costs rise faster than loan yields, net interest income shrinks even though rates are higher.
Show when: Interest expense growth > interest income growth
